deliverables.text: A wind-vector table covering every waypoint on both routings: the wind at cruise level written first as a magnitude and a direction, and then resolved into east and north components, with the full conversion shown for at least one entry.

A course unit-vector table covering every leg of both routings: each leg's true course expressed as a unit vector in east and north components, with the calculation that shows the resulting vector's magnitude is exactly one.

A wind-component table: for every leg, the dot product of that leg's wind vector with that leg's course unit vector, in knots, under a stated sign convention for headwind versus tailwind, with the crosswind component reported alongside it.

A wind-triangle diagram and ground-speed table for every leg: the true-airspeed vector, the wind vector, and the resulting ground vector drawn head to tail and added, with the ground speed reported as the magnitude of that sum.

A trip fuel table for both routings — leg time, leg fuel, route total, the reserve check, and pounds of fuel per nautical mile of net progress toward the destination — plus a break-even calculation: by what percentage would the forecast headwind component along The Great Circle have to be wrong for the two routings to cost the same fuel?

appendices.title: Aircraft, Performance, and the Fuel Rule

balance.argument_a: The extra track miles on The Southern Swing are certain and are paid on every leg: Routing A's filed track is 2,266.3 nm against Routing B's 2,402.7 nm, 136.4 nm (6.0%) of extra distance that Routing B has to earn back purely on wind. The amount of forecast error that erases it -- a uniform 7.2 kt per leg, a 20.5% overstatement of Routing A's along-course headwind components -- is not merely asserted as ordinary: published peer-reviewed verification research on jet-stream-level winds (Schafler et al. 2020, Monthly Weather Review [S8]) documents individual-case wind-speed errors up to +/-10 m/s (~19.4 kt) in numerical weather prediction analyses and short-range forecasts, concentrated in upper-level ridges above the tropopause -- the same structure that produces this case's own strongest forecast winds. That study verifies a different jet and forecast system (North Atlantic, ECMWF/Met Office) than the NWS FD product this case cites, so it is not a direct measurement of this issuance's error -- but it is real evidence that errors several times the case's 7.2 kt/leg break-even are a documented, non-exotic feature of jet-stream-level forecasting, not a rare tail event. Argument A's claim is therefore not that Routing B's saving is fake or that Routing A is the lower-variance choice (it is not -- see exposure asymmetry below), but that a 472.8 lb / 1.67% margin sits inside a documented noise band this large, and a single 12-hour-old forecast issuance is not solid enough ground to spend 136 certain nm chasing a saving that small.
balance.argument_b: Under the wind field the National Weather Service actually published for this date and valid period, the along-course headwind component at KDBQ is -74.8 kt, dropping Routing A's first-leg ground speed to 384.7 kt against a 460 kt true airspeed. Routing B never sees an along-course headwind worse than -8.6 kt and picks up a +9.4 kt tailwind component on its final leg. Trip fuel is 27,756.2 lb for Routing B against 28,228.9 lb for Routing A - 472.8 lb cheaper, 1.67% on the primary metric, despite flying 136.4 nm further. Fuel is bought by the hour, not by the mile, and the published forecast is the product a dispatcher is required to plan against.
balance.margin_basis: (worse routing's trip fuel - better routing's trip fuel) / worse routing's trip fuel x 100, where trip fuel = sum(filed leg distance / leg ground speed) x cruise fuel flow and each leg's ground speed is sqrt(TAS^2 - crosswind^2) + along-course wind component, both components obtained by projecting the sourced wind vector onto the leg's course unit vector. Both routings fly the same type at the same true airspeed and the same fuel flow, so the ranking is decided entirely by sourced distances (S1/S2) and published winds (S3) plus MA2's stated allowance; S5's fuel-flow figure scales the answer but cannot change which routing wins. Computed value: 28,228.9 lb (A) vs 27,756.2 lb (B) -> margin_pct 1.67, Routing B cheaper.
balance.twist_effect: A line of convective weather closes the KSGF corridor and Routing B must be re-filed via KMEM - a waypoint whose position and forecast wind are already published in Appendices A and B, so the room can recompute it. Routing B's filed track grows from 2,402.7 nm to 2,467.0 nm and its trip fuel from 27,756.2 lb to 28,410.4 lb, which is 181.4 lb MORE than Routing A's 28,228.9 lb. The verdict flips: Routing A becomes the cheaper plan by 0.64%. Every position that was held on 'the southern route is cheaper' is invalidated, and the new margin is thinner than the old one. Verified mechanically by evaluate_twist() in sensitivity_model.py. Honest caveat, disclosed in MA2: at the low end of MA2's +/-50% flex range for the southern corridor (0.75% instead of 1.5%) the reroute does NOT flip the verdict - the twist's direction depends on a stated assumption, and the Guide Notes say so.
balance.stability: Stable under a +/-50% flex of every stated Modeling Assumption: Routing B stays cheaper across the whole sweep, margin 0.95%-2.40%, no flips, no breach of the SPEC section 2 20% cap (Tier 2 probe 5). GENUINELY FRAGILE to the cited wind data, which is the case's own headline finding rather than a defect: a 20.5% uniform overstatement of Routing A's along-course headwind components flips the verdict. Per case-readiness's own rule, cited measurements are stress-tested by probe 6, not probe 5 - but the fragility is disclosed here, in MA2, in D5's break-even deliverable and in FACILITATOR.md so no guide defends a margin that is sturdier than it is.

cohort_bands.note: The Socratic plan and anchor timings in FACILITATOR.md run as written (0:00-45:00). Anchor 1's stand-up vote is a real split worth reading, and all three deep-conflict threads run. Split the room into two dispatch desks for the Data Deep Dive — one works Routing A's three legs, one works Routing B's — and have them trade tables before D5.

Anchors 2 and 3 combine into one pass ('what are we actually comparing, and how'). Run one deep-conflict thread only — certain cost versus forecast benefit, which needs the least setup. The twist still drops at 15:00. Do not split the room into two desks; work one leg of each routing together on the board and let the rest be homework. Total runtime about 30 minutes.

There is no vote to take at Anchor 1 — the learner states an initial position instead of a hands-up split, and the guide argues the other routing directly rather than cold-calling. The twist still lands, but 'who reverses' becomes 'would you reverse, and why'. Skip the deep-conflict threads and go from the twist recommit straight to Close, spending the recovered time on D3's dot product, which is the single hardest step to do alone.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Meridian's frequency on this city pair, used only to annualise the per-flight difference
modeling_assumptions.value_used: 2 departures per day, 365 days a year (730 departures)
modeling_assumptions.basis: Meridian Air is fictional; no schedule for it can exist publicly. Two daily frequencies is an ordinary mainline transcontinental pattern.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Scales the annual dollar figure linearly. Cannot change which routing wins - it multiplies both routings by the same number.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Airway-structure allowance: the percentage by which filed track miles exceed the great-circle distance
modeling_assumptions.value_used: +1.0% on the northern corridor (Routing A), +1.5% on the southern corridor (Routing B)
modeling_assumptions.basis: A real, well-known effect - filed routings follow published airways and fixes, not an exact great circle - with no published per-corridor figure. The southern corridor is given the larger allowance on the reasoning that it offers fewer direct routings and more weather deviation. That direction is asserted, not measured, and a Hero may reasonably argue the opposite.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Directly load-bearing and the single largest stated lever in the case. Flexed +/-50% one dial at a time in Tier 2 probe 5: Routing B stays cheaper throughout, margin 0.95%-2.40%; at the joint corners of the two dials the band is 0.46%-2.88% and Routing B still wins every corner. Reversing the two values WIDENS the gap to 2.64% rather than narrowing it. It is also load-bearing on the TWIST: at the low end of Routing B's flex range (0.75%) the twist's reroute no longer flips the verdict (Routing B stays cheaper by 0.10%). The twist half is disclosed in the facilitator-only half of case.md and in FACILITATOR.md, deliberately not in MA2's student-facing sensitivity column, which would leak the amendment.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: One wind vector per leg, taken at the leg's downwind-end waypoint and held constant along the whole leg
modeling_assumptions.basis: A real flight-planning system samples the forecast grid continuously. Holding one published point wind per leg is what makes this case computable by hand.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Understates how much the wind varies along a long leg. It hits Routing A's 957.4 nm KDBQ->KSLC leg and Routing B's 936.0 nm KJFK->KSGF leg hardest, and those two are roughly the same length, so the simplification does not obviously favour one routing. Non-numeric: flexed by hand, not by probe 5.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Density of Jet A used to convert pounds of fuel to US gallons
modeling_assumptions.basis: The planning density used throughout US aviation. The governing specification (ASTM D1655) is paywalled and no US-government page stating a pounds-per-gallon figure was located and fetched in this session - so this is declared as an assumption rather than cited. See RESEARCH_LOG.md, P71.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Affects only the dollar figure, and affects both routings identically. Cannot change which routing wins.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Leg geometry: each leg's length is the great-circle distance between its endpoints, while its true course is the INITIAL great-circle course of that leg, held constant end to end
modeling_assumptions.value_used: applied to all six legs of both routings and to the KSFO->KLAX alternate leg (non-numeric)
modeling_assumptions.basis: A great circle's true course changes continuously along the leg - on the 957.4 nm KDBQ->KSLC leg it runs from 271.4 deg at the start to 257.2 deg at the end. Holding the initial course constant is the standard hand-planning simplification and is what makes a single dot product per leg meaningful. A track flown on a genuinely constant true course is a rhumb line, which on these legs is longer than the great circle by roughly a tenth of a percent, so the two halves of the assumption pull slightly against each other. Added at Tier 2 probe 4 on 2026-08-12: case.md Appendix A had cited 'SEE APPENDIX E, MA5' since case-write while no MA5 existed.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Load-bearing on every along-course and crosswind component (D3, D4) and the least conservative assumption stated. Re-solving the whole case on mean-of-initial-and-final courses gives margin 2.01%, on final courses 2.27%, on true rhumb-line courses with rhumb-line distances 2.06%, against the base 1.67% - Routing B is cheaper under every one. The twist still flips under all of them, but by as little as 0.08% on final courses. Non-numeric: flexed by hand, not by probe 5.

facilitator.twist: Forty minutes to push, a line of thunderstorms goes up across the Ozarks and the corridor through Springfield is shut. If the dispatcher still wants the southern plan he has to re-file it through Memphis instead, which is further again. Both waypoints are already in his corridor file, so he can price it - he has about a minute to decide whether the southern plan is still the plan.
facilitator.twist_source: Uses only data already published in Appendices A and B (KMEM position and its 34,000 ft forecast wind). No new number is introduced by the twist.
facilitator.trap: Heroes will compare the routings on the wind's raw published speed rather than its component along the course, and will skip the projection entirely; and they will default to comparing distance flown instead of time aloft.
